name: Kalima
label: Factory Records
lede: Six Manchester teenagers rehearsed next to Joy Division as Swamp Children, borrowed most of A Certain Ratio, renamed themselves after an Elvin Jones tune and ended up as regulars at Gilles Peterson's Sunday sessions.

eras.title: Swamp Children, aged 16 to 19
eras.text: The kids shared a rehearsal room with A Certain Ratio and Joy Division, learned fast, and fell in with Manchester's jazz-funk clubs. By 1982 they had a five-star album and a slot in a London 'new jazz' season.

years.h: Swamp Children start in a room shared with Joy Division
years.p: [[Ann Quigley|8099c4cd-8107-4b91-9bb9-79fb5683c570]], [[Tony Quigley|183ca605-2760-46b6-9098-515918c9d3a3]], Ceri Evans, Cliff Saffer, [[Martin Moscrop|0966e7ae-08f3-4923-adda-1a220212264d]] on drums and John Kirkham, the only one with a band behind him ([[Pink Military|a18ca853-1943-4c50-8df2-e241cea1d230]]), rehearse for six months beside [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]] and [[Joy Division|9a58fda3-f4ed-4080-a3a5-f457aac9fcdd]].
years.xp: The members were between 16 and 19. Kirkham had also auditioned for [[Ludus|81a3daeb-dfad-4ff3-80dc-0fcf793e2db7]]. Ann Quigley had already used the name Swamp Children for a one-off fanzine she largely made herself.

years.h: U2 drive over from Dublin and get bumped for Swamp Children
years.p: The band's first show is at Manchester's Beach Club. LTM's history says a double booking meant [[U2|a3cb23fc-acd3-4ce0-8f36-1e5aa6a18432]], who'd travelled from Dublin for the slot, were turned away.

years.h: Two producers, one from each side of the Pennines
years.p: Swamp Children cut 'Boy' at [[Cabaret Voltaire|439a29ad-f4ef-4857-a7cd-3d4a551056c8]]'s Western Works in Sheffield, co-produced by A Certain Ratio's [[Simon Topping|6dd95305-7ca6-464d-a9de-93c3a963cda9]] and Cabaret Voltaire's [[Stephen Mallinder|adad4d39-c1e6-4533-b4dc-76e6ac328299]].

years.h: NME loves them at Heaven, Sounds calls them immature
years.p: At a Les Disques du Crépuscule showcase at Heaven in London with Marine and [[Richard Jobson|402264b1-972e-4196-ae86-e53be140620c]], NME's Leyla Sanai hears a true mix of 'Nouveau Fun(k)'. Sounds' Chris Burkham isn't sold.

years.h: Little Voices, Fac 49, the first Factory record
years.p: Swamp Children's debut 12-inch EP on Factory Records.

years.h: Crépuscule's boss asks for a Factory Benelux single
years.p: Michel Duval invites the band to record Taste What's Rhythm, with the ballad 'You've Got Me Beat'. A live take from the Haçienda on June 29 lands on the Factory Outing video.

years.h: So Hot lands five stars in the Virgin Rock Yearbook
years.p: Recorded in August. Melody Maker's Frank Worral called it one of the best records of the year.
years.xp:
Highlights were 'Samba Zippy', 'El Figaro' and 'Secret Whispers'. Worral praised its "shimmering kaleidoscopic brightness".

The same August the band played the ICA in London as part of The Joy of Mooching, a season for the new jazz scene that also had Weekend, Animal Nightlife and Carmel. At home, they were regulars at Fevers, Legends and Berlin, where DJs Hewan Clarke and Colin Curtis were spinning jazz-funk.

eras.title: A Certain Ratio, played in 7/8
eras.text: Renamed Kalima, the band took in almost all of A Certain Ratio and moved toward bossa nova and Latin jazz, playing Ronnie Scott's and WOMAD. It got big, eight players plus a manager, and too big to pay for.

years.h: Swamp Children become Kalima, after an Elvin Jones track
years.p: The name comes from 'Kalima' on [[Elvin Jones|d5ac66e4-ea5d-4ebb-9e0d-bed4063208e7]]'s 1978 album Remembrance. Percussionist Chris Manis, pianist [[Andy Connell|b57d99e1-5149-418b-8194-09db8782edb7]] and bassist Jez Kerr join.
years.xp: LTM notes the new line-up took in most of [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]], all but drummer [[Donald Johnson|49569ee1-aba3-4c08-8ead-9791a7f8c96d]]. By early 1985 Tony Quigley had joined ACR too, and the two bands split the work: harder sounds in ACR, jazz in Kalima.

years.h: 'Fly Away' is a bossa nova in 7/8
years.p: Kalima's first Factory single, Fac 87, pairs a Sarah Vaughan-style 'The Smiling Hour' with the original 'Fly Away', in the odd time signature that became their trademark.

years.h: With ACR in America, the rest play as the Kalima Quartet
years.p: While [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]] tour the US, Kalima's remaining players do experimental acoustic sets as a quartet. Elsewhere the full band plays Ronnie Scott's, the Wag, WOMAD and the Bracknell Jazz Festival.

years.src: LTM: Kalima · LTM: Night Time Shadows
years.h: Night Time Shadows tightens up for the dancefloor
years.p: The debut album, Fact 155: 'After Hours', 'Start the Melody', 'In Time'. Record Mirror heard moody after-hours jazz with a velvety voice.

q: The departure of Martin, Jez, Andy, Ceri and Nathan marked the end
years.h: Andy Connell joins Swing Out Sister, and the ACR wing follows him out
years.p: Connell leaves for [[Swing Out Sister|d12b5853-71eb-41d9-8d18-a4259477848a]]'s chart run; Jez Kerr, Martin Moscrop and Ceri Evans go too. Manager Nathan McGough leaves to manage the [[Happy Mondays|01f4fb92-6bf0-4de5-83dc-3fe194e763bf]].
years.xp: By 1986 Kalima had eight players and a manager, which LTM says the band couldn't afford to keep. The April single Whispered Words (Fac 147) was the last release by the original line-up.

eras.title: Fans in Japan, Sundays at Dingwalls
eras.text: A rebuilt Kalima found a second audience: acid jazz in London and record buyers in Japan. Then Factory, flush from Madchester, moved into expensive new offices, and the band's best-reviewed record in years didn't sell.

years.h: 'Weird Feelings' and a new bassist
years.p: The rebuilt band, with Martin Hennin on bass and guest trumpeter Khairie Ghadal, releases Fac 187. Warren Sharples, drummer David Higgins and percussionist Andy Boothman soon settle in, with Matthew Taylor and Bernard Moss on horns.

years.h: New Order's engineer produces Kalima!
years.p: Fact 206, recorded late in 1987 with Michael Johnson. The album wins the band fans in Japan and on London's acid jazz scene.

years.h: Sundays at Dingwalls with James Brown's horn players
years.p: Kalima become regulars at [[Gilles Peterson|4c4e3121-4d12-4f7a-a77c-5becd849fb3c]]'s Sunday sessions in Camden, on bills with [[Pee Wee Ellis|6fd0f3e6-e490-449a-8573-f8f1fe551c8d]] and Haji Akbar from James Brown's horn section, and with [[Flora Purim|b1091eee-4198-4e66-8b15-05ae12b03353]] and [[Airto Moreira|dd2abaa1-0b73-4ded-82ed-c80cce8d6378]].

years.h: Flyaway collects the singles
years.p: A compilation, FACD 219. In NME, Dele Fadele argued the biggest misconception about Kalima was that they were simply jazzy.

years.h: Gilles Peterson remixes 'Shine' into a club hit
years.p: Feeling Fine (Fact 249), produced by Tim Oliver, is all self-written. The 'Shine' 12-inch, with remixes by Oliver and by Peterson and Patrick Forge, does well in the clubs.
years.xp: Drummer Ian Kelly came in for the album. Jazz FM and Blues and Soul backed it, and LTM calls it the band's strongest since Night Time Shadows.

years.big: "Never got the credit. Blame the company."
years.h: Tony Wilson takes the blame for Feeling Fine
years.p: Factory moves into expensive new city-centre offices and Feeling Fine doesn't sell outside its niche. In his sleevenotes for the Palatine retrospective, [[Tony Wilson|124a6f5d-b2e0-4a75-95ad-db4c38063e02]] owned it.

years.h: After a Boardwalk show, Ann and John take a break
years.p: Following a gig at Manchester's Boardwalk with Ashley and Jackson, Ann Quigley and John Kirkham step back. Tony Quigley carries on in [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]]; Factory goes under at the end of 1992.

eras.title: Three of the six, on their own label
eras.text: The Quigleys and Kirkham came back as a trio for one more album, on a label of their own, while LTM put the Swamp Children and Kalima catalogue back into print.

years.h: Ann and Tony Quigley and John Kirkham make In Spirit
years.p: Kalima's fourth album, on their own Kin label (KIN-001), promoted with a few trio shows.

years.h: LTM reissues everything but Feeling Fine
years.p: Between 2004 and 2005 LTM Recordings put out all the Swamp Children and Kalima recordings on CD, including Night Time Shadows + Singles, except the last Factory album.
